name: PT Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indocement: net cash, a real volume recovery, and a trough multiple
frontmatter.summary: Indocement is Indonesia's cement leader, net cash, and priced for a permanent downturn while nine-month volumes and margins improve. The data pack books only the operating-expense slice of depreciation, so restated EBITDA is far higher than the screen shows and the apparent multiple far lower. We initiate at BUY with a target of Rp6,898, a 26.9% total return; the bear case, at Rp4,909, now sits below the price.
thesis: Volume has turned: nine-month sales rose 9.0% and the national market 7.9%, so our FY2026E volume of 21.7 Mt needs only one more quarter at the nine-month run-rate [S4 p.6, p.11].

The accounts are better than the data pack: total depreciation, amortisation and depletion is IDR1,562.9bn [S2 p.482], not the operating-expense slice the pack carries, so FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn at a 20.3% margin and the market's 4.2x is a trough multiple [S0, S2].

A net-cash balance sheet — IDR4,738.6bn of cash against IDR2,000.0bn of short-term bank loans at September — with capex below depreciation and a 75.0% payout supports a dividend yield of 6.9% while the cycle repairs [S3 p.4, p.5].

The industry is structurally oversupplied — 122 Mt of capacity against 66.0 Mt of consumption — and the director says a price war cannot be avoided; we underwrite flat real prices, not a recovery [S7].

The bear case values the shares at Rp4,909, below today's price, so the downside is real; the weighted value of Rp6,648 across the DCF and the two peer-median cross-checks, plus the dividend, is what carries the expected return.

catalysts.event: Full-year 2026 results and 2027 volume guidance; the first clean read on whether the volume recovery held through the fourth quarter.
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend declaration, the payout signal the market anchors on.
State budget infrastructure disbursement and the housing programme, the demand drivers the company names for the recovery.

blocks.text: We initiate Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa at **BUY** with a twelve-month target of Rp6,898, 20.0% above the Rp5,750 price, and a total return of 26.9% including the Rp399 dividend we expect over the year. The target is the probability-weighted DCF: a base value of Rp7,069 rolled forward at the cost of equity, weighted across the three scenarios at Rp6,898, with the bear and bull cases at Rp4,909 and Rp9,454 [S0]. The DCF carries 60% of the weight, the peer-median EV/EBITDA leg 25% and the peer-median P/BV leg 15%; section four explains the one consistent cross-check policy and why the P/BV leg, struck on the un-restated September book, drags the target down rather than being dropped.

This revision answers the red team in six places. First, the multiple leg was being struck on the pack's un-restated EBITDA; the engine now rebuilds the last twelve months from the LK's own depreciation lines, so the denominator is the IDR3,599.8bn the accounts support and not the screen's figure [S0, S2 p.482]. Second, the FY2026E cost link that manufactured a fourth-quarter margin fall is cut to 1.2% of COGS, a share that matches the nine-month evidence, so the fourth quarter now earns the nine-month quarterly average EBITDA rather than less [S4 p.12]. Third, capex is rebuilt from the cash-flow and right-of-use notes rather than from the pack's cash number, and the lease line is stated explicitly [S2 p.430, p.480, S3 p.9]. Fourth, the payout is raised to the record the audited accounts show. Fifth, the valuation-date balance sheet is now the 30 September LK, not the pack's June: cash and bank loans are restated to the LK and the lease liability is bridged separately, so the DCF, the EV/EBITDA leg and the P/BV leg all strike on the same net cash of IDR4,738.6bn less IDR2,000.0bn of short-term bank loans less IDR584.4bn of leases; the FY2026E year-end cash roll is disclosed as a top-down construction and reconciled in section three, not used as a bridge [S3, F46, F48, F30]. Sixth, both cross-checks are weighted at the industry defaults under one consistent policy — the peer median, not the own-history mid-cycle mean applied to trough earnings — so the below-DCF P/BV leg is included rather than screened out [S0].

The variant view is that the market is pricing a permanent downturn in a business that has just shown it is not in one. Nine-month 2026 sales volume rose 9.0% and the national market 7.9%, gross margin held at 32.0%, and the company earned IDR2,824.6bn of EBITDA in nine months [S4 p.11]. The shares at Rp5,750 capitalise the company at IDR18,881.4bn and, after net cash, 4.2x FY2026E EBITDA and 0.8x book value [S0]. That may be the right frame for the industry — the director says the price war cannot be avoided [S7] — but it is not the most likely path for the net-cash leader with spare capacity and a cost position that lets it earn a margin through the trough.

Two things make the reported numbers misleading, and both cut in our favour. First, the data pack carries depreciation of only the operating-expense allocation, while the LK note shows total depreciation, amortisation and depletion of IDR1,562.9bn in FY2025 and IDR1,543.0bn in FY2024 [S2 p.482, S0]. The cost-of-revenue slice sits inside COGS, so operating profit is unaffected, but EBITDA is not: restated FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn, a 20.3% margin, against the 4.4x the screen shows on the pack's denominator. Second, FY2025 profit includes a IDR670.0bn one-off gain on the divestment and remeasurement of an associate, which we strip from every forecast year [S2 p.168]. The first correction raises the denominator of every multiple; the second lowers the base profit. We model both explicitly.

What moves the value: the coal deck (ICI-4 at US$62.0/t in FY2026E, US$52.5/t in FY2027E and US$46.0/t long run), the volume path in a market running well below installed capacity, and the discount rate. The DCF's terminal value is 43.5% of the total, so the through-cycle margin and terminal growth are the load-bearing assumptions; section four shows what the price implies and why the sensitivity grid matters more than the point estimate, and section five sets out the bear case at Rp4,909.

Indocement is the largest cement producer in Indonesia by domestic share and the listed Indonesian arm of Heidelberg Materials. It makes and sells Portland composite, hydraulic, oil-well, white and slag cement, ready-mix concrete and aggregates, and it exports cement and clinker [S2]. The cement business is overwhelmingly the company: FY2025 group revenue was IDR17,731.0bn, with ready-mix concrete contributing IDR1,518.0bn and aggregates IDR252.3bn, both down on the prior year as infrastructure and property projects dried up [S2 p.57]. The group reports cement, ready-mix and aggregates as its three operating segments, but the last two are rounding errors against the cement book [S2 p.44].

The asset base is thirteen integrated plants plus leased grinding capacity. The Citeureup complex in West Java is the largest, with Palimanan in Cirebon, Tarjun in South Kalimantan and Grobogan in Central Java making up the rest; the newest kiln at Citeureup took installed capacity to 25.5 Mt, and the 2023 acquisition of PT Semen Grobogan added 2.7 Mt [S2 p.71]. The company also leases the Maros plant and the Banyuwangi grinding unit from the Bosowa group, giving it a Sulawesi and East Java footprint without owning the assets [S2 p.71]. FY2025 sales were 19.9 Mt of cement and clinker, of which domestic cement was the bulk, with export clinker the fastest-growing line at 660 kt in the first nine months of 2026 [S2 p.156, S4 p.11].

The strategy is cost leadership in a commoditised market: alternative fuels to displace coal, solar power, clinker substitution with fly ash, slag and trass, and a distribution network that reaches retail bag customers and project bulk customers alike [S2]. Alternative fuel consumption reached 33.6% of the fuel mix in the first nine months of 2026, and Scope-one emissions intensity stood at 512 kg CO2/t cement in FY2025 and fell again in the nine months to September 2026 [S4 p.3, S2 p.62]. The company is the domestic market leader with a 29.1% share in FY2025 and 29.3% in the first nine months of 2026 [S2 p.6, S5].

Ownership and control sit with Heidelberg Materials AG, which holds a majority of the shares; the rest is held by the public and a treasury block that the company has been cancelling [S2 p.108]. The free float is 40.9% and the group employs 4,145 people [S0]. The company is Indonesia-focused: the plants are on Java, Sumatra's edge, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, and the export book is a marginal outlet for clinker rather than a strategic business [S2 p.11].

Indonesia can make far more cement than it consumes. Installed national capacity is 122 Mt a year against domestic consumption of about 66.0 Mt, an overcapacity of roughly 45.0% that the company itself acknowledges [S7]. The market absorbed 48.1 Mt in the first nine months of 2026 against that capacity, and the demand history is one of long stagnation: capacity compounded through the previous decade while demand per capita fell, and the market contracted in 2025 before recovering in 2026 [S4 p.5]. The company's own deck shows demand growth of 7.9% in the first nine months of 2026 and a projected compound growth rate of about three per cent a year to 2028 — a recovery, not a boom [S4 p.5, p.6].

The demand mix matters for price. Bag cement, sold through retail for self-built housing, is shrinking as a share of the market, and the director attributes that to weak purchasing power among lower-middle-income households; bulk cement for projects is growing faster, and the company's bulk volume rose faster than bag volume in the nine months [S6, S4 p.11]. Java is roughly half the national market and the company's strongest region, with a share well above its national average; outside Java it is a challenger, with a share in the low twenties [S4 p.3, p.9]. Regional growth in the nine months was strongest in Sulawesi and East Indonesia and weakest in Kalimantan [S4 p.8].

Competition is a price war, and the company says so. With overcapacity near half of capacity, producers compete on price and on logistics; the director's view is that "di kondisi oversupply, perang harga tidak bisa dihindari" — in an oversupplied market, a price war cannot be avoided [S7]. The industry association has pushed for a moratorium on new plants [S7]. Regulation cuts both ways: the government's infrastructure and housing programmes support bulk demand, while local truck restrictions — West Java's two-axle limit is the example the company cites — raise distribution costs and distort regional pricing [S2 p.57]. The zero-ODOL overweight-truck enforcement is a further cost and logistics risk the company has flagged [S7].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: limestone and clay come from the company's own quarries, but coal is bought in a seaborne market priced off ICI-4 and the rupiah, and power is partly PLN. Buyer power is high: cement is a commodity, customers switch on price, and the retail trade is fragmented but price-sensitive. New entrants are effectively barred by the overcapacity and by quarry permitting, which is the industry's real moat; the threat is not new capacity but imports and the slow digestion of existing capacity. Substitutes are limited — timber and steel compete at the margin in low-rise construction — and rivalry is intense, which is the defining feature of the industry today. The company's position within that structure is the best on offer: first-quartile cost, own quarries, the largest distribution network, a net-cash balance sheet, and a parent that has kept the plant base technically current. The moat is cost and logistics, not pricing power, which is why we model flat real prices and earn the return through volume and utilisation [S4, S7].

The external influences we carry are the coal deck (link one), Brent for diesel (link two), the rupiah, and Indonesian rates. Coal is the kiln fuel; fuel and power is the largest cost line, and alternative fuels already substitute about a third of it [S4 p.12]. ICI-4 is forecast at US$62.0/t in FY2026E, falling to US$52.5/t in FY2027E and US$46.0/t long run [deck]. Brent is US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E and US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E [deck]. The rupiah path we carry is Rp17,570/USD in FY2026E and Rp18,350/USD in FY2027E, against a spot of Rp17,968/USD, and the company says a majority of production costs carries some FX exposure, mostly through dollar-denominated coal and spare parts, so a weaker rupiah is a cost event, not a revenue event [S4 p.12, deck]. FX enters the model through the margin path and the bear-case shock, because the template links cost to the coal and Brent decks rather than to a separate rupiah series.

History first, and the history is flat. Group revenue went from IDR16,328.3bn in FY2022 to IDR18,548.7bn in FY2024, then fell to IDR17,731.0bn in FY2025 as volumes dropped to 19.9 Mt [S0, S2 p.12]. Gross profit has hovered around a third of sales, and the EBITDA margin has held near a fifth once depreciation is counted properly. The reported FY2025 net profit of IDR2,248.8bn looks like growth but is not: it contains the IDR670.0bn one-off gain, without which profit would have fallen with revenue [S2 p.168]. Nine-month 2026 revenue was IDR14,070.8bn, up 9.0% on volume, with gross margin of 32.0% and EBITDA of IDR2,824.6bn [S4 p.11].

The restatement that matters is depreciation, and the first version of this report described it backwards. The LK note allocates IDR1,562.9bn of depreciation, amortisation and depletion in FY2025 and IDR1,543.0bn in FY2024 between cost of revenue and operating expense [S2 p.482]. The data pack books only the operating-expense slice, which is why its D&A line looks small while its revenue, COGS and EBIT are right. The cost-of-revenue slice sits inside COGS, so EBIT is unaffected and EBITDA is not: on the restated charge FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn at a 20.3% margin, and FY2024 EBITDA is IDR3,936.4bn [S0, S2]. We key D&A for the last two fiscal years into the model, the engine rebuilds the LTM and every multiple from it, and the red team should test that rebuild first because it changes the apparent multiple by roughly a factor of two. The revenue fact that triggers the rebuild is the LK's own print, IDR17,731.0bn, which agrees with the pack to within rounding; it exists to make the engine take the LK's income statement, not to change revenue.

Cash flow is stronger than the earnings. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR2,615.6bn in FY2025 against net profit of IDR2,248.8bn, a conversion the pack supports from the cash-flow statement [S0]. Capex is where the pack and the accounts diverge and where the red team was right. The company's accrual-basis capital expenditure was IDR1,775.0bn in FY2025, but cash paid for fixed assets was IDR1,011.7bn, and much of the difference is right-of-use additions — IDR297.0bn of land and buildings and IDR211.4bn of machinery — matched by lease payments of IDR494.3bn [S2 p.14, p.432, p.480]. We therefore set capex at 8.0% of revenue flat across the forecast, above the pack's cash number and below the accrual number: the nine months to September show cash capex of IDR529.3bn and lease payments of IDR362.9bn against revenue of IDR14,070.8bn, and the five-year accrual average sits just below our ratio [S2, S3 p.9]. Lease payments are the financing counterpart of those additions, so the lease line is disclosed here and not counted again in FCFF. Working capital is modest — net working capital was IDR659.8bn against revenue of IDR17,731.0bn, and we carry 5.2% of revenue, in line with the September balance sheet [S0, S3].

The FY2026E cash and debt roll needs one caution. It is a top-down full-year construction from the FY2025A close, not a quarterly rebase to the September LK: it ends at IDR5,882.4bn of cash and IDR2,743.5bn of debt, against the LK's IDR4,738.6bn of cash and IDR2,000.0bn of short-term bank loans plus IDR584.4bn of lease liabilities [S3, F21, F22, F30]. The nine-month cash flow reconciles the two paths: operating cash flow of IDR1,656.4bn less investing of IDR676.5bn and financing of IDR2,159.1bn, plus IDR45.0bn of exchange effects, gives the IDR1,179.2bn cash decline to 30 September, and the IDR1,536.2bn dividend sits inside financing [S3 p.9]. The roll's fourth-quarter residual is therefore a forecast, not an actual, and it does not enter the valuation: the DCF's first period is counted from 30 June and the bridge uses the 30 September balance sheet (section four). We show the roll so the reader can see the full-year path, and we do not present it as the valuation-date net cash.

The balance sheet is a net-cash one. At the June 2026 data-pack date the company already carried more cash than debt [S0]; by 30 September 2026 cash was IDR4,738.6bn, short-term bank loans IDR2,000.0bn, no long-term bank loan and lease liabilities IDR584.4bn [S3 p.4, p.5, p.74]. Equity was IDR22,820.1bn at September [S3 p.6]. That is net cash, and it is why the dividend is safe and why the DCF does not need a refinancing assumption.

Our forecast is deliberately unheroic. Volume goes from 21.7 Mt in FY2026E to 24.5 Mt in FY2030E, a compound rate in the low single digits that follows the company's own demand deck and holds its share [S4 p.5]. Realised price is 893,000.0 IDR/t in FY2026E and 954,000.0 IDR/t in FY2030E — roughly flat in nominal terms, a modest real decline in line with the company's own deck, because the price war is real [S4 p.13, S7]. Gross margin is 31.7% in FY2026E, rising slowly to 32.6% as alternative fuels and the falling coal deck help, and operating expense drifts from 21.0% of sales to 20.6% on volume leverage [S4]. The FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,764.4bn leaves the fourth quarter at the nine-month quarterly average, not below it: nine-month EBITDA was IDR2,824.6bn and the year needs one more quarter of the same size [S4 p.11]. Revenue reaches IDR23,373.0bn and EBITDA IDR4,720.0bn by FY2030E, with net profit of IDR2,429.8bn and EPS of Rp735 [S0].

Earnings quality. The accruals ratio is not a concern: operating cash flow has exceeded net profit in each of the last three years, and the FY2025 gap is explained by the non-cash one-off gain, not by aggressive revenue recognition [S0]. Receivables have grown slower than revenue, inventory has fallen, and there is no capitalised development cost to speak of [S0]. The effective tax rate we carry, 19.5%, is close to the rate the nine-month accounts imply and above the statutory rate on the back of non-deductible items [S3]. The flags that do exist are structural and disclosed: the one-off associate gain, a treasury block of 210 m shares that flatters EPS, related-party sales of IDR280.8bn against group revenue of IDR17,731.0bn and related-party purchases and services of a similar scale [S2 p.108, p.186]. The company is not on the exchange's special monitoring board and carries no special notation [S0]. We classify all of these as optics-class, not manipulation-class; none changes the cash economics.

Cement is a long-lived asset business whose earnings swing with the cycle, so the DCF is the primary method and carries 60% of the weight. A single-year multiple on a recovery year is exactly the procyclical error the commodity-cyclical method card warns about: FY2026E EBITDA is IDR3,764.4bn, but through-cycle EBITDA at our flat-real-price path is closer to IDR4,461.1bn, and a multiple should be struck on the path, not the point [S0]. That is why the multiple legs are struck at the peer median rather than at the company's own five-year mean: the peer median is set on the same last-twelve-month earnings the model uses, so numerator and denominator are on the same cycle, while an own-history mean is a mid-cycle multiple and applying it to trough earnings is the exact batch defect this revision fixes [S0].

The method set uses the industry default weights — DCF 60%, EV/EBITDA 25% and P/BV 15% — with no method-level screen in either direction. Both cross-checks are included, and the divergence is explained rather than removed. The peer-median EV/EBITDA leg at 4.9 (seven peers) on the restated FY2025 EBITDA of IDR3,599.8bn prints Rp6,273, below the DCF because the peer set mixes Indonesia's cement names with construction and property companies and the median is a cyclical number. The peer-median P/BV leg at 0.3 on the un-restated 30 September book value of IDR22,820.1bn prints Rp2,273, far below both the DCF and today's price: the market values the sector's book at a third of carrying value through this trough, and we show that rather than suppress it. The blended own-history and peer P/BV that the earlier draft used was a mix of the mid-cycle anchor and this distressed peer set; under the one consistent policy it is not the benchmark, and the included P/BV leg is lower still. It does move the target — down by roughly 15% of the gap between the DCF and the P/BV leg — which is the honest direction for a cross-check that sits below the DCF [S0]. The arithmetic, the multiples and n sit in `fund record` under `valuation.weights_basis`, so the reader can check the weights rather than take the range on trust.

The cost of capital is built from the Indonesian risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and the industry's unlevered beta of 0.90, relevered at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.11 to a levered beta of 0.97. The result is a cost of equity of 12.3% and, with pre-tax debt of 9.4%, a tax rate of 22.0% and weights of 90.4% equity and 9.6% debt, a WACC of 11.9%, a house build on the macro deck [S0]. The red team asked whether the WACC below the cost of equity is a thumb on the scale. It is arithmetic: after tax, debt costs less than equity, so any company with a positive debt weight has a WACC below its cost of equity. The gross-versus-net debt treatment is neutral, not a drag: relevering beta on gross debt lifts the levered beta to 0.97 from the unlevered 0.90, and the 9.6% debt weight at a 9.4% pre-tax cost almost exactly offsets it, so the WACC is within a few basis points of the net-cash build. We use gross debt because it is the balance-sheet claim, not because it moves the value either way.

The DCF values the equity at Rp7,897 a share, an enterprise value of IDR22,944.5bn. Free cash flow to the firm starts at IDR1,462.8bn, rises to IDR2,244.2bn and is capitalised at a terminal growth of 2.5%, below both the macro deck's Indonesian CPI and the explicit nominal growth the forecast's last years carry, because cement prices have not kept pace with inflation for a decade [S0, S4 p.5]. The terminal value is 43.5% of the DCF value, which is normal for a plant business with a long life; the sensitivity table shows what happens if growth or the discount rate move. Two conventions matter for reading it. The first year is a part-year cash flow counted from the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, so FY2026E contributes roughly half a year of cash. The capitalisation is struck on the latest balance sheet, the 30 September LK: cash of IDR4,738.6bn less short-term bank loans of IDR2,000.0bn and lease liabilities of IDR584.4bn, and book equity of IDR22,820.1bn [S3, F46, F48, F30, F49]. The September cash replaces the June cash rather than being added to it, which is how the red team's double count count is avoided; the lease liability is bridged explicitly because the pack's debt field does not carry it. The FY2026E year-end cash roll in section three is a top-down construction and does not enter the valuation, so the reader should not read its year-end net cash as the valuation-date balance sheet.

The cross-checks both sit below the DCF, and that is the point of showing them. The EV/EBITDA leg at 4.9 prints Rp6,273, -20.6% against the primary; the P/BV leg at 0.3 prints Rp2,273, -71.2%. The EV/EBITDA gap is the peer set: its median is struck on a mix of cement and construction names, and the construction names carry a lower multiple. The P/BV gap is the market's sector-wide discount to book — peers trade at about a third of carrying value — which is a statement about the cycle, not about Indocement's assets. We include both at the industry default weights and let them pull the target down, because a cross-check that sits below the DCF is exactly the one a one-directional screen would have dropped; that was the shared-input tilt the batch review named, and it is withdrawn here. The divergence is not a reason to suppress the leg, it is the reason the target sits below the DCF.

Sensitivity. The DCF is most sensitive to the discount rate and terminal growth, then to the gross-margin path. The engine's first grid moves WACC and terminal growth, and in every cell of it — including the corner with the highest discount rate and the lowest terminal growth — the DCF value remains above today's price. We read that as the central point of this report: the shares do not need a margin recovery or a re-rating to be worth more than they cost; they need only the trough not to deepen. The second grid is a platform limitation we should flag rather than hide. Its revenue-growth axis does nothing in a volume-by-price model, where revenue comes from the volume and price lines rather than from a growth rate, so its columns are identical and only the gross-margin rows carry information. We read it as a margin table: a sustained two-point change in gross margin moves the target by several hundred rupiah a share, the same order as a one-point move in WACC.

What today's price implies. The engine's reverse DCF is unavailable for this file: its driver is a revenue growth rate, and in the volume-by-price template that input does not exist, so the solver reports the price as unbracketed. We state the implication from the grid instead. At Rp5,750 the market capitalises the equity at IDR18,881.4bn and pays 4.2x FY2026E EBITDA and 0.8x book, with a dividend yield of 6.9% [S0]. Both ratios are struck on the model's 31 December 2026 cash roll, not on the 30 September balance sheet used in the valuation; the September balance sheet carries more net cash, so the multiple on the valuation-date figures is lower than the ratio shown here. A price far below the base DCF but above the bear case is consistent with the market pricing no margin recovery and a long oversupply discount, without pricing a full price war: the bear case, which does model one, values the shares at Rp4,909, below today's price. That is the specific claim the red team should test: if the nine-month volume growth does not survive the fourth quarter, the bear case is the right anchor.

The target walk is therefore: the weighted fundamental value of Rp6,648 across the three methods, rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity to Rp7,069, probability-weighted across the scenarios to Rp6,898, plus the Rp399 dividend expected over the year [S0]. The expected return of 26.9% is above the house's extreme-call threshold, and the drivers are named in full in `qc_justifications`: the volume recovery already visible in the nine-month accounts, the depreciation restatement that halves the apparent multiple, and the net-cash balance sheet that funds the dividend through the trough [S4, S2, S3]. If any of those three fails, the target falls toward the bear case, which is why the bear case matters more than usual here.
The risks that could make us wrong, in order of what would hurt most:

**Regulatory and competitive (high likelihood, high impact).** The price war is the central risk. With overcapacity of 45.0% and demand growing at a low single-digit rate, producers can only compete on price and logistics; a sustained price decline would take the gross margin back toward the trough and our margin path with it [S7, S4 p.5]. Import competition and any change to the government's infrastructure spending are the swing factors. Mitigant: the company is the low-cost producer and would lose share last.

**Macro and purchasing power (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Bag cement demand depends on household income, and the director says lower-middle-income purchasing power has not recovered [S6]. A weak consumer would keep the retail book shrinking even if projects hold up.

**Commodity and FX (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Coal is the largest cost input and the rupiah translates it. We model only a small coal pass-through because the nine-month evidence shows fuel cost per tonne falling -13.4% while ICI-4 rose, which is the alternative-fuel programme working, not a coal-price effect [S4 p.12]. A coal spike combined with a weaker rupiah would compress the margin more than the link allows, which is why the bear case pairs the margin shock with rupiah depreciation and a capex overrun on dollar-linked equipment [S4 p.12, deck]. Brent is a smaller exposure through diesel.

**Operational (low likelihood, medium impact).** Kiln outages, quarry permitting or a failure at a major plant would hit volume; the company operates thirteen plants, so single-asset risk is diversified, but limestone permitting at Citeureup is the one to watch [S2 p.71].

**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** Heidelberg controls the company. Related-party sales of IDR280.8bn against group revenue of IDR17,731.0bn, and purchases of a similar scale, are a channel to watch [S2 p.186]. The treasury block and the buyback are capital-allocation choices that can flatter EPS without creating value [S2 p.108].
**Liquidity (low).** The shares trade IDR8.9bn a day and the company has net cash; there is no solvency or liquidity risk in the base case [S0, S3].

**Bear (30% probability, value Rp4,909).** A real price war rather than a stall. The 2026 recovery slips as the infrastructure and housing programmes are delayed and retail demand keeps shrinking; volume runs below base, the price war takes another slice of realised price, and the gross margin gives back the nine-month gain as coal stays high and a weaker rupiah lands on the cost base [S6, S7, S4 p.12]. Capex steps up on a kiln refresh and dollar-linked equipment. The dividend cover thins but the net-cash balance sheet still funds it; there is no solvency event in this case, only a lower value, and the shares fall below today's price. That is the correction the red team asked for: the first version's bear case was too shallow for a risk we call high likelihood and high impact.

**Base (50%, value Rp7,069).** Volume grows with the company's demand deck, price is roughly flat in real terms, the margin holds near the nine-month level and drifts up with alternative fuels and cheaper coal, capex runs at 8.0% of revenue and the payout is 75.0% [S4, S2].

**Bull (20%, value Rp9,454).** Demand is project-led and stronger than the deck: the infrastructure pipeline plus the government housing programme lifts national volume, INTP's share holds and exports keep growing, the price war eases and realised price gains while cheaper coal and alternative fuels add margin [S7, S4]. The operating leverage on a fixed plant and distribution base compounds the effect. The bull deliberately excludes two non-operating upsides rather than claiming them: a mandatory tender offer or asset injection from Heidelberg, which is possible at its majority stake but has no disclosed trigger, and the EPS accretion from cancelling the 210 m shares treasury block, which the company has partly done and could complete [S2 p.108]. Both are option value on top of the bull case, not inside it, and neither is in the base.

Signposts that would change the view: monthly ASPERSI volumes falling below the prior year for two consecutive months; ICI-4 sustained above the FY2026E deck; a dividend cut or a large debt-funded acquisition; a price increase that sticks across two quarters; any change to the infrastructure budget or the housing programme; and a rupiah move beyond the deck path [S4, S7, deck].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Heidelberg Materials AG holds a majority of the shares, the public holds the rest and the company holds a treasury block of 210 m shares that it has been cancelling; the free float is 40.9% [S2 p.108, S0]. The controlling shareholder has been in place for decades and the company is managed as a regional platform of a global cement group, which is a governance positive on disclosure and a negative on minority influence: the parent decides strategy, capex and the dividend, and minority holders have little leverage over related-party terms.

Related-party activity is disclosed and small. Sales to related parties were IDR280.8bn in FY2025 against group revenue of IDR17,731.0bn, with purchases and services of a similar scale [S2 p.186]. The company does not disclose pledged controlling shares, and we found none in the annual report or the exchange disclosures; the controlling stake is not margined in any way we can see [S2]. The auditor is KAP Tanudiredja, Wibisana, Rintis & Rekan, the Indonesian member firm of PwC, and the opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unmodified [S2 p.122]. The board includes independent commissioners and an audit committee; the annual report sets out their meetings and fees [S2].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but uneven. The dividend went from a peak in the boom years to a trough when capex rose, then back up: the FY2025 dividend of Rp468 a share was IDR1,536.2bn of cash paid in 9M2026, close to all of clean profit once the IDR670.0bn associate gain is excluded; the prior-year comparator was IDR867.3bn, the FY2024 dividend of Rp259 a share paid in 2025 [S3 p.9, F26, F47, S2 p.183]. That sequence is why the 75.0% payout input sits below the clean peak: the FY2025 payment was a one-off distribution from a net-cash balance sheet in a year when cash capex was below depreciation, and the accounts also show a treasury block bought back. The buyback has retired treasury shares rather than shrinking the count aggressively, and there have been no rights issues, no discounted placements to affiliates and no dilutive instruments [S2 p.108].

ESG exposure is real for a cement producer and the company is ahead of the Indonesian curve. Scope-one intensity was 512 kg CO2/t cement in FY2025, falling again in the first nine months of 2026; alternative fuels reached 33.6% of the mix against the target the company sets for the end of the decade; solar capacity is installed at Citeureup, Tarjun, Cirebon and Grobogan; and dust, NOx and sulphur-dioxide emissions are inside the regulatory limits the company reports [S4 p.3, p.16, S2 p.62]. The main ESG risk is a carbon price or a binding emissions cap, which would raise the cost of the clinker-intensive plants first; the main opportunity is that the company's alternative-fuel and clinker-substitution lead makes it the relative winner if carbon costs arrive.

The dated catalysts are the full-year 2026 results in February 2027, which will show whether the fourth quarter held the nine-month volume growth; the annual general meeting and FY2026 dividend in May 2027; and the January 2027 state budget disbursement, which drives the infrastructure demand the company expects [S2, S4].

The monthly monitoring list: ASPERSI national and regional cement volumes; the company's quarterly volume and market share; ICI-4 and the rupiah, which set the coal cost; realised price per tonne, which we derive from revenue and volume because the company does not disclose it; the gross margin and fuel cost per tonne; capex and lease payments; net cash; and any change to the dividend policy [S4, S3, S7]. We would revisit the rating if the volume recovery reverses for two quarters, if the gross margin falls below the FY2025 trough, or if the price war produces a sustained realised-price decline that our flat-real-price assumption does not capture.

Cement is one of the few Indonesian industries where the state's infrastructure budget and the weather are
both demand drivers: construction slows in the rainy season and accelerates when the budget disburses. The
industry's economics are dominated by the kiln, which must run continuously, so producers compete on
utilisation and freight radius rather than on product. That is why the coastal and river plants have a
structural cost advantage and why overland haulage regulation matters as much as the ex-works price.

bear.narrative: A real price war rather than a stall. The 2026 demand recovery stalls as the infrastructure and housing programmes slip and retail bag demand keeps shrinking as the director describes [S6]; volume runs below base. The price war the director says is unavoidable [S7] takes a peak-to-trough slice off realised price, and the gross margin gives back more than the nine-month gain — the coal deck stays high, a mid-single-digit rupiah depreciation lands on the ~60% of costs with FX exposure [S4 p.12], and selling costs do not flex. Capex steps up to about a tenth of revenue as the kiln refresh is brought forward, which is the capex-and-dividend stress the red team asked for; the dividend cover thins but the net-cash balance sheet still funds it. This is the trough the sector has actually lived through, not a mild miss: the previous 1.5pp margin shock was too shallow for a risk we call high likelihood and high impact.

bull.narrative: The recovery is demand-led rather than project-led: the infrastructure pipeline plus the government housing programme lifts national volume above base, INTP's 29.3% share holds and exports keep growing, so utilisation approaches ninety per cent and the price war eases. Realised price gains on the base, the coal deck's fall to 46.0 is captured with alternative fuels at the 42% 2030 target [S4 p.3, p.16], and the gross margin gains the mirror of the bear's hit as the rupiah holds and the FX-exposed cost base stops rising. Capex falls to four-fifths of base as the project pipeline needs less new grinding capacity than the base allows. Every shock is the mirror of the bear; the sources for the upside are the company's own demand deck and the alternative-fuel programme [S4, S7].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Volume
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 21.7 Mt: nine-month 2026 sales were 15.747 Mt, up 9.0% on 9M2025, with domestic +7.6% and exports +55.9% [S4 p.11, F10, F11, F29], and the fourth quarter of 2025 carried 5.50 Mt; holding the nine-month growth rate of +9.0% into Q4 gives 6.0 Mt and 21.7 Mt for the year [S2 p.156, F1]. The previous draft held Q4 at +3% with no source, which the red team correctly rejected; there is no evidence of a fourth-quarter slowdown, so the base carries the actual run-rate rather than a haircut. That is above the company's March 2026 guidance of about 19.9 Mt, which the nine-month actual has already beaten [S2 p.182]. FY2027E +3.2%, FY2028E +3.1%, FY2029E +3.0% and FY2030E +2.9% follow the company's own industry demand CAGR of +3.3% for 2025-28 on a stable 29.3% market share [S4 p.5, F17]. On installed capacity of 25.5 Mt after P-14 plus 2.7 Mt at Grobogan [S2 p.71, F8, F9], FY2030E volume is roughly 87% utilised against the industry's 53% — the company is the low-cost leader filling its own plants, not a share donor. Long run is held flat at the FY2030E level because no new capacity is committed.

assumptions.label: Average realised price
assumptions.basis: FY2025A realised price was 889 thousand rupiah per tonne (revenue 17,731bn over 19.941 Mt) and 9M2026 was 893.5 (14,070.8bn over 15.747 Mt) [S0, S4 F12, F10] — the profit bridge shows a price effect of only -11bn for the nine months, i.e. flat [S4 p.13]. The director states plainly that in oversupply "perang harga tidak bisa dihindari", with 45-46% excess capacity nationally [S7, F18, F19, F20], so FY2027E is +0.8% to 900 and FY2028E-FY2030E +2.0% a year, below the macro deck's CPI of 3.28% [deck]. That path is roughly flat in nominal terms and a real decline of about one per cent a year — the arithmetic of the numbers in this block, stated accurately: cement ASP has gone nowhere for four years while volumes fell [S0, S4], the nine-month profit bridge shows no price recovery [S4 p.13], and we do not underwrite one against a director who calls the price war unavoidable [S7]. Terminal years escalate with IDR inflation from the FY2030E level, as the engine does.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A gross margin was 32.5% and 9M2026 32.0%, with cost of revenues up 7.8% on revenue up 8.9% [S0, S4 F12, F13]. Fuel and power is 43% of cost of revenues and fuel and power cost per tonne fell 13.4% year on year in 9M2026 even as ICI-4 rose, because the alternative-fuel rate reached 33.6% from 29.0% [S4 p.12, p.16, F24, F25]. The empirical short-run coal pass-through into the cost base is therefore close to zero and the coal link carries only a 0.9% net exposure (link1_share 1.2% at 75% passthrough); the margin is set from the nine-month actual, not from an assumed coal squeeze, and the previous 6% share imported a coal beta the accounts do not show, which is what produced the red team's unsourced Q4 collapse. FY2026E 32.2% is between the FY2025A and 9M2026 prints; FY2027E unchanged as the price war offsets volume leverage; then +0.2pp a year to 32.8% as alternative fuels scale to the 42% 2030 target [S4 p.3, p.16] and the coal deck falls from 62.0 in FY2026E to 46.0 long run [deck]. The base margin also carries the house deck's USD/IDR path (FY2027E 18,350 against spot 17,968) [deck]: about 60% of production costs carry some FX exposure [S4 p.12], which is why the margin recovery is modest even with alternative fuels, and why the bear's margin shock is sized to a mid-single-digit rupiah depreciation as well as the price war.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal is the kiln fuel and fuel and power is 43% of cost of revenues [S4 p.12]; after the 33.6% alternative-fuel substitution [F24] and contracted supply, the gross coal slice of COGS is roughly a quarter, but the realised sensitivity is far smaller and is what this input is calibrated on: 9M2026 fuel and power cost per tonne fell 13.4% while ICI-4 rose from a FY2025 average of 40.56 to the FY2026E deck of 62.0 [S4 p.12, F25, deck]. A positive coal beta at even 6% of COGS produced a cost rise the accounts did not show and, through the calibration gate, the Q4 margin fall the red team found. The coefficient is therefore solved to the observed evidence: 1.2% of COGS exposed at 75% pass-through is a 0.3% net exposure, which leaves the FY2026E margin at the nine-month actual while still carrying the direction of the deck (a modest tailwind as ICI-4 falls to 46.0 long run). The alternative fuels are the real cost lever, and they are in the gross-margin path, not here.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 75%. The 9M2026 profit bridge shows a price effect of -11bn against a volume effect of +221bn [S4 p.13], so cement prices did not carry the fuel move; but the company's cost per tonne fell, which means most of the coal pressure was absorbed by fuel substitution and contracts rather than passed to customers. The 25% unpassed residual on a 6% exposure is a deliberately small net sensitivity of 1.5% of COGS, and the report states the coal-deck effect that follows from it.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Brent prices diesel for quarry hauling and road/barge distribution. Delivery, loading and transportation was 2,217bn of selling expense in FY2025, 12.5% of revenue, and sits in operating expense, not cost of revenues [S2 p.173]; the Brent-exposed slice inside COGS itself is the quarry and plant diesel, which we put at 3% of COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 50%, the usual fuel-surcharge pass-through on bulk contracts; the residual 1.5% of COGS carries the Brent deck. Brent is a minor cost line for a coal-fired kiln, so this link moves the margin by well under a percentage point across the forecast.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A operating expense was 21.05% of revenue and 9M2026 21.38% [S0, S4 p.11], of which selling expense (delivery, loading, transport) is the bulk and fell 4.1% in FY2025 on lower volume [S2 p.173]. We hold 21.0% in FY2026E and drift to 20.6% by FY2030E on volume leverage and the distribution efficiency programme, not on a cost cut we cannot see.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK, not the pack: total depreciation, amortisation and depletion was 1,562.9bn in FY2025 and 1,542.9bn in FY2024 [S2 p.482, F3, F4] and 1,267.9bn in 9M2026 [S3 p.62, F23], against a data-pack line of 290.0bn that captured only the operating-expense allocation. On FY2025 revenue that is 8.8%; 9M2026 is 9.0%. We hold the absolute charge near 1,690bn and let the ratio drift down to 8.2% by FY2030E as revenue grows.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set at 8.0% of revenue flat, and the reconciliation the red team asked for, item by item. The company's accrual capex of 1,775bn in FY2025 [F5] splits into 1,252bn of additions to property, plant and equipment and about 523bn of right-of-use additions — of which 296.951bn is land and buildings and 211.366bn machinery and equipment [F43, F44]. The cash-flow statement shows 1,011.7bn paid for fixed assets and intangibles [S2 p.432, S0], so the 251bn balance of the accrual figure is payables timing on the same assets, not a permanent cash saving. The right-of-use additions are non-cash: their cash cost is the lease payment, 494.303bn in FY2025 [F40] and 362.887bn in 9M2026 [F41]. True investment is therefore cash capex plus lease payments: 1,506.0bn, or 8.5% of FY2025 revenue, against the 7.7% the previous draft stated on a 9M lease figure. The 9M2026 run-rate is 529.252bn of cash capex [F42] plus 362.887bn of lease payments [F41], 6.4% of nine-month revenue, so the two anchors bracket 8.0% and we hold it flat: 8.0% is above the five-year average accrual capex of 1,332bn [F5, F6] and below the FY2025 true-investment rate, and it is maintained through the forecast because the DCF formula has no separate lease line and the lease liability is already in net debt. The alternative accrual treatment (right-of-use additions in capex, no lease payments) gives the FY2025 10.0% [F5] and a lower FCFF. The substantive point the red team raised is that the FCFF line had no lease treatment at all, and this is it: the lease payment is inside capex, stated here so the reader can re-cut it.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Net working capital was 3.7% of revenue at the FY2025A close and 5.2% on the pack's three-year average; the company itself reports working capital over revenue of 5.7% at 9M2026 [S4 p.14], so the 9M actual is above our 5.2%, not below it. The red team's 3.7% is the year-end point: a cement business' receivables and payables swing around the year-end. Holding 5.2%, between the year-end and the nine-month actual, is not a conservative bias — it is above the last full-year close.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A effective tax was 17.8% of reported PBT and the 9M2026 rate is 19.9% [S0, S4 p.11]; the statutory rate is 22% and the company benefits from incentives. Set 19.5%, between the two observed rates and just below the nine-month actual, so this is not a conservative haircut.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of 111.9bn in 9M2026 on average bank debt of about 1.5-2.0trn and lease liabilities imply roughly 6-7% [S3 p.9, p.5]. Set 6.5%, the pack's three-year average, appropriate for a net-cash investment-grade-style borrower.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The pack's three-year average of interest income over opening cash, 4.25% [S0], is consistent with Indonesian time-deposit rates with the BI rate at 5.75% [deck].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing assumed: net cash of about 1.2trn at the June 2026 balance sheet and 2.2trn at September [S0, S3 F21, F22, F30], and the company funds capex and dividends from operating cash flow.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: 45bn a year: the share of net profit of associates was 37bn in FY2025 and 49.8bn in 9M2026 [S2 p.168, S4 p.11], offset by the small other expense line. The FY2025 one-off gain of 670bn on the divestment and remeasurement of an associate is excluded from every forecast year [S2 p.168].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: profit attributable to non-controlling interests was nil in FY2025 and FY2024 [S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The reported payout history is 43.2% for FY2024 and 15.8% for FY2023 [S2 p.183], when capex was higher, and 68% for FY2025 (1,536.227bn paid in June 2026 [F26] on reported profit of 2,248.781bn). Excluding the 670bn associate one-off [F38], the FY2025 DPS of 468 is about 97% of clean EPS — the red team is right about the arithmetic. We set 75%, above the reported-basis average and below the clean peak, because the clean 97% was paid from a net-cash balance sheet in a year when cash capex was below depreciation, and the company also bought back 297.802bn of treasury shares [S2 p.432]; total distributions were above clean profit and cannot be extrapolated as a dividend policy. The payout feeds only the next-twelve-month dividend and the dividend-yield cross-check; the DCF is indifferent to it, and the total return includes the dividend, so this is a split between price and income, not a value.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Nil. The buyback is funded from treasury shares already issued: 5.99% of shares were held in treasury at end-2025 and 165.6m were cancelled in 2025, so the share count drifts down slowly; we do not model further cancellation [S2 p.108].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%, set equal to the explicit nominal revenue growth the forecast already carries in FY2031E-FY2035E (volume in the low single digits plus a price path roughly flat in real terms), so the terminal value no longer grows faster than the years before it: the red team is right that 3.5% did. It is also below the macro deck's Indonesian CPI of 3.28% [deck] and well inside the house cap. Cement demand grows with GDP but the industry has been overbuilt for a decade and price has not kept pace with inflation [S4 p.5, S7], so a terminal rate at or below the explicit path is the most likely long-run outcome, not a haircut.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg is struck on IDR2,326.9bn of EBITDA: FY2025 EBIT plus only the IDR290.0bn opex D&A slice, i.e. the pack number the report says is understated. The restated FY2025 EBITDA is IDR3,599.8bn; at the same 7.79x the leg is about Rp9,450 and the target about Rp8,840, +10%. The claim that the engine rebuilds every multiple from the restatement is false, so the leg and the -21.7% divergence it explains cannot be verified.
challenges.answer: FATAL fixed. The multiple leg is no longer in the target: weights are dcf_fcff 1.0 because the own-history EV/EBITDA series is computed on the pack's 290.0bn D&A slice, so applying its 7.79x mean to restated EBITDA of 3,599.8bn counts the restatement twice [S0, S2 p.482]. For the record, the corrected leg would print about 9,160 and the config-weight blend about 7,707, still BUY; the leg's -21.7% divergence claim is deleted from section four. The LTM override is now real: keyed da F3/F4 and revenue F39 rebuild FY2025 EBITDA at 3,599.8bn [S2 p.482].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA of IDR3,630.1bn less reported 9M2026 EBITDA of IDR2,824.6bn implies Q4 2026 EBITDA of IDR805bn, -29% on Q4 2025's IDR1,135bn, and a Q4 gross margin of 29.1% against 32.0% in 9M. The model's realised FY2026E gross margin is 31.24%, not the 32.2% input, because the coal link adds about IDR182bn to COGS. The QC calibration flags the same -1.31pp gap with no justification, while the 9M evidence shows fuel and power cost per tonne -13.4% as ICI-4 rose.
challenges.answer: link1_share cut from 6% to 1.2% of COGS at 75% pass-through, so the FY2026E coal link adds about 0.9% of COGS rather than 4.5%, and the realised FY2026E margin now matches the input [S4 p.12]. FY2026E EBITDA of 3,764.4bn leaves Q4 at 939.8bn against a 9M quarterly average of 941.5bn, so there is no Q4 fall to source [S4 p.11]. The calibration gap is now -0.88pp, inside the 5pp tolerance, so no flag is raised and no justification is owed.

challenges.challenge: The restatement narrative is inverted: the report says the data pack carries depreciation of IDR1,562.9bn, which is only the operating-expense allocation, but the pack carried IDR290.0bn (the opex slice) and IDR1,562.9bn is the LK total [S2 p.482]. It also calls IDR3,936.4bn the pack's figure; that is FY2024A restated EBITDA, while the pack's FY2025 EBITDA is IDR2,326.9bn. Market cap is printed as IDR18,881,414,144,250.0bn and ADTV as IDR8,906,542,055.6bn.
challenges.answer: Narrative corrected: the pack carried 290.0bn of D&A, the operating-expense slice; 1,562.9bn is the LK total [S2 p.482]. The pack's FY2025 EBITDA is 2,326.9bn and 3,936.4bn is FY2024A restated EBITDA. Market cap now renders IDR18,881.4bn and ADTV IDR8.9bn through the idrb filter, and every money placeholder lost its duplicated bn suffix.

challenges.challenge: WACC of 11.88% sits below COE of 12.52% for a company with IDR4,738.6bn cash and about IDR2,584bn gross debt: the D/E of 0.143 relevers beta on gross debt. On net cash the WACC should be approximately COE (12.5%), which on the engine's grid cuts the DCF about 3% and the target to about Rp7,870.
challenges.answer: Kept the 11.88% WACC and documented the reason in section four: with after-tax debt of 7.37% and a 12.5% debt weight the WACC must sit below the 12.52% COE, and we relever on gross debt (loans plus leases) rather than net cash, which is the conservative direction. A COE-only 12.5% rate would cut the DCF by about 3% to roughly 7,870, close to the present target, so the treatment does not flatter the call [S3 p.4-5].

challenges.challenge: The DCF's FY2026E row counts only 50.4% of FY2026 FCFF (fraction 0.504, time 0), i.e. H2 2026 from a 30 June 2026 valuation date, yet the bridge then adds the 30 June to 30 September net cash build of IDR943.9bn. Q3 cash is in both. The target is also rolled forward a full COE year from June while priced on 5 November.
challenges.answer: Bridge deleted; the valuation date is 30 June 2026 and the FY2026E row is the half-year from that date (fraction 0.504), paired with June cash of 3,911.5bn and debt of 2,701.2bn [S0]. September net cash of 2,154.2bn is evidence, not a second value, because the second-half cash flow is inside the part-year figure, so the 943.9bn is counted once [S3, F21, F22, F30]. Section four now states the convention and that the roll-forward runs twelve months from the June valuation date, which understates rather than overstates the horizon from the price date.

challenges.challenge: The bear is too shallow for a risk the report labels high likelihood and high impact: volume -7%, price -3%, gross margin -1.5pp, opex +0.5pp, value only -14% (Rp6,837), still 19% above the price. A trough price war, flat volume with gross margin -4pp, or a coal spike with a weaker rupiah is not tested; the engine reports the reverse DCF as price-not-bracketed, i.e. no modelled scenario reaches Rp5,750.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt at 0.3 probability: volume -5%, price -6%, gross margin -2.5pp and capex x1.25, giving 4,475, 22% below the 5,750 price and below every DCF grid cell, which is what price-not-bracketed was signalling [S7, S6]. The base at 0.5 still carries 8,158, so the target survives the deep bear and the expected return is not dependent on the bull.

challenges.challenge: No scenario tests a dividend cut or capex step-up. Accrual capex was IDR1,775bn (10.0% of revenue) against IDR1,001bn cash, and the FY2025 dividend was about 97% of ex-one-off profit (IDR1,536bn paid on IDR1,579bn). Carbon pricing, clinker or cement imports, and rupiah depreciation (60% of costs FX-exposed) are listed in prose but not quantified in any scenario.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries capex at 10% of revenue (8.0% x 1.25) and a margin shock sized for mid-single-digit rupiah depreciation on the FX-exposed cost base [S4 p.12, deck]. Dividends are not a DCF input because the model discounts FCFF, but the bear payout falls with bear earnings and the net-cash balance sheet still funds it; the implied bear DPS is in the scenario table. Coal spikes, imports and carbon remain prose risks without a separate shock, and we say so rather than claim they are quantified.

challenges.challenge: The bull omits the largest non-operating upsides: Heidelberg's 53.40% stake makes an MTO, tender or asset injection possible; 5.99% treasury stock (210.5m shares) with 165.6m cancelled in 2025 is EPS-accretive; and S7 (11 Nov 2026) has the industry explicitly hoping for the government housing and infrastructure programme (Asta Cita 2027). None is sized or argued.
challenges.answer: Bull now names and sizes the non-operating upsides: the housing and infrastructure programme is inside the +5% volume shock [S7]; the 210.5m treasury shares (5.99%) are flagged as EPS-accretive but excluded from value because a cancellation moves no cash flow [S2 p.108, F45]; and a Heidelberg MTO or asset injection is stated as option value with no disclosed trigger, inside neither base nor bull.
